In this manuscript, the authors investigated the function of REDD1 in regulating obesity-
induced endothelia cell (EC) senescence and hypertension. They found that HFD feeding
increased REDD1 expression in aortic endothelium in mice and obesity promote EC
senescence in a REDD1-dependent manner. They further revealed that REDD1 plays a
central role in the pathogenesis of obesity-induced EC senescence and hypertension by
stimulating NF-κB-dependent miR-155-5p/214-3p expression, which leads to the
downregulation of eNOS and SIRT1 expression. The manuscript included comprehensive in
vitro and in vivo data. However, there are several issues with the mouse models the authors
used and the described underlying mechanisms. I have the following specific comments:
Comment #1: The authors showed that systemic delivery of Ad-REDD1 but not Ad-REDD1KKAA
induces EC senescence and hypertension. It is not clear whether Ad-REDD1 and Ad-REDD1KKAA
can efficiently target other tissues in addition of aorta. What is the tissue distribution pattern of
Redd1 or REDD1KKAA after delivery? REDD1overexpression has been shown to stimulate
preadipocyte differentiation and proinflammatory cytokine expression through atypical IKK-independent
NF-κB activation in adipose tissue (Nat Commun. 13, 6303 (2022)). If Ad-REDD1 and
Ad-REDDKKAA delivery also led to increased RREDD1 or REDD1KKAA expression in adipose
tissue, this may affect the obesity and its’s associated phenotypes. The authors need to
characterize the obesity and metabolic phenotypes carefully in those mice.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. To address the concerns
regarding tissue distribution and potential metabolic effects, we analyzed REDD1 expression
across multiple tissues and measured circulating obesity-related factors in mice injected with
Ad-REDD1 or Ad-REDD1KKAA. The new data are presented in Supplementary Fig. 8a/b and
described in the revised Results section (Lines 186–192) as follows: “To investigate the in vivo
role of REDD1 in vascular dysfunction, male mice were intravenously injected with Ad-REDD1
or Ad-REDD1KKAA. In both groups, Redd1 mRNA levels were comparably upregulated across
most tissues, showing the highest levels in the liver, markedly increased expression in the
heart and aorta, and minimal expression in adipose tissue (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Serum
levels of obesity-related factors, such as leptin, resistin, and triglycerides, showed no
significant changes, whereas TNF- was elevated only in Ad-REDD1-injected mice
(Supplementary Fig. 8b).”
(2) These findings indicate that adenoviral delivery did not induce major obesity-related or
metabolic changes, minimizing the potential confounding effects from adipose tissue. Instead,
14
the results support a specific role of REDD1 in promoting endothelial senescence and
hypertension.
Comment #2: In Fig. 5, the authors showed Redd1 deficiency prevents DIO-induced EC
senescence and hypertension. Again, did Redd1 deficiency affect the DIO directly? Obesity
and metabolic phenotypes of those mice under chow and HFD feeding condition need to be
characterized.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for this important comment. Because it has been
previously reported that Redd1–/– mice exhibited protection against obesity and metabolic
phenotypes compared with WT mice under HFD feeding (Ref. 20), we further analyzed
circulating obesity-related factors under lean and DIO conditions in three mouse models: WT
versus Redd1KKAA, Redd1fl/fl versus Redd1ΔEC, and WT versus miR-214-3p–/–. Consistent with
a previous study in DIO-Redd1–/– mice (Ref. 20), obesity-related factors were significantly
reduced in Redd1KKAA mice compared with WT controls under DIO conditions. In contrast, no
significant differences were observed between Redd1fl/fl versus Redd1ΔEC mice or between WT
and miR-214-3p–/– mice. Importantly, these parameters showed no significant differences
between genotypes under lean conditions.
(2) These results suggest that the vascular protective effects observed in Redd1ΔEC and miR-
214-3p–/– mice are not due to changes in obesity or metabolic phenotypes, but rather reflect
the direct role of endothelial REDD1 in promoting vascular senescence and hypertension.
(3) The new data are presented in Supplementary Fig. 10a–c, and the Results section has
been updated accordingly (Lines 260–263, 275–277, 299–300).
Comment #3: The authors generated EC-specific Redd1 mouse model which could address
some of above concerns. However, the manuscript did not include basic characterization of
these mice. Did deficiency of Redd1 in ECs protect mice from DIO, systemic inflammation,
and other metabolic disorder. It is plausible that those factors can contribute indirectly to the
observed EC senescence and hypertension phenotypes.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for this important point. A prior study reported that
Redd1–/– mice exhibited protection against meta-inflammation compared with WT mice under
DIO conditions (Ref. 20). As described in the response to Comment #2, we also analyzed
serum TNF- levels under lean and DIO conditions in three mouse models: WT versus
Redd1KKAA, Redd1fl/fl versus Redd1ΔEC, and WT versus miR-214-3p–/–. DIO increased serum
TNF- levels in WT mice, which was prevented in Redd1KKAA mice, but not in Redd1ΔEC or
miR-214-3p–/– mice; under lean conditions, no significant differences were observed between
15
any of the genotypes and WT mice.
(2) These results indicate that the vascular protective effects observed in Redd1ΔEC and miR-
214-3p–/– mice occur independently of systemic inflammatory changes.
(3) The new data are presented in Supplementary Fig. 10a–c, and the Results section has
been updated accordingly (Lines 260–263, 275–277, 299–300).
Comment #4: miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p have been well known to play diverse roles in
regulating various gene expression and are also linked to cancer, inflammation, and many
physiological processes. The authors should explore how the changed miR-155-5p and miR-
214-3p affect the different gene/pathways in addition to eNOS and SIRT1. For example,
experiments would give a better overview of the impact of miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p on EC
gene expression. Do other genes/pathways contribute to observed EC senescence or
dysfunction?
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for highlighting the broader roles of miR-155-5p and
miR-214-3p beyond SIRT1 and eNOS. Although we did not perform RNA-seq in this study,
previous studies, including RNA-seq data, have shown that these miRNAs regulate multiple
genes and pathways that influence endothelial senescence and vascular dysfunction.
(2) Regarding additional targets and pathways of miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p beyond SIRT1
and eNOS, we have added the following statement to the Discussion section (Lines 433–440):
“However, additional targets and pathways cannot be excluded. For instance, miR-155-5p
may regulate the senescence-associated TERF1–p21/p16 axis53, while miR-214-3p may
influence quaking-dependent vascular pathways, including the downregulation of
TERT/TERF1–p21/p16 and VEGFA/bFGF50,54. Notably, RNA-seq analysis of miR-214-3p-
knockdown cells revealed upregulation of numerous genes associated with angiogenesis, cell
proliferation, and cell migration52. Collectively, these findings suggest that miR-214-3p impairs
endothelial function not only through the suppression of eNOS and SIRT1 but also via
additional target genes that regulate vascular homeostasis.”
(3) We also incorporated the following information into the limitations section of Discussion
section (Lines 478–479): “Finally, additional targets of miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p should be
identified using RIP-seq or CLIP-seq approaches that exploit target site complementarity.”
In this study, authors analyzed the roles of REDD1 in mediating endothelial dysfunction due
to obesity, and found that REDD1 promotes NF-κB signaling, which alters eNOS and SIRT1
via miR-214-3p. This mechanism is lengthy and possibly REDD1 can directly exert effects on
endothelial cells considering that REDD1 is a stress protein known to induce senescence.
There are several major problems:
Comment #1: The evidence supporting the involvement of NF-κB signaling is weak. Also, NF-
κB signaling is a generic inflammatory pathway which can induce many changes, not only
miR-214-3p and others.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for this important comment. Additional experiments
showed that obesity-related factors, palmitic acid and oxLDL increased miR-155-5p and miR-
214-3p levels in HAECs and MAECs. This induction was effectively inhibited by NF-κB p65
knockdown and substantially reduced by REDD1 or IKKβ silencing, although residual miRNA
levels remained significant (Supplementary Fig. 7; Lines 176–183). These results indicate that
REDD1-dependent atypical NF-κB activation serves as an important upstream driver of
miRNA biogenesis, although IKK-dependent NF-κB signaling also contributes.
(2) Moreover, an additional experiment using the IKK inhibitor Bay 11-7082 showed that
canonical NF-κB signaling is also activated but less critical under DIO conditions (Fig. 6a–h;
Supplementary Fig. 9a, b; Lines 240–256). The interplay between atypical and canonical NF-
κB pathways may further exacerbate EC senescence and vascular dysfunction by enhancing
miRNA biogenesis and cytokine expression (Fig. 10g; Lines 330–340).
(3) Supporting evidence includes several key observations: NF-κB p65 knockdown, but not
IKKβ silencing, attenuated REDD1-mediated NF-κB activation and miRNA expression,
eNOS/SIRT1 downregulation, and EC senescence (Fig. 2h, i; Supplementary Fig. 4d, e);
overexpression of REDD1, but not the NF-κB-inactive mutant REDD1KKAA, increased miRNA
levels and EC senescence (Fig. 3j–m); and DIO-induced vascular dysfunction occurred in WT
mice but was significantly reduced in Redd1KKAA mice (Fig. 7).
(4) NF-κB is a key driver of cellular senescence (Refs. 2, 29, 31) and may regulate multiple
downstream targets beyond miR-155-5p/miR-214-3p, including NF-κB-responsive or obesity-
associated miR-31-5p, miR-34a-5p, and miR-130a-3p, which may influence EC function via
NF-κB, eNOS, and SIRT1 (Refs. 5, 10, 55–57). However, our qRT-PCR analysis additionally
reveal that these miRNAs were not significantly elevated in the aortic tissue of DIO-WT mice
(Supplementary Fig. 13; Lines 444–449), suggesting that they may not be critically involved
in REDD1-dependent or obesity-mediated EC senescence and vascular dysfunction.
17
(5) REDD1-induced NF-κB activation itself can induce EC senescence independently of
miRNAs. Although not directly examined, we discuss this possibility in the revised manuscript
as follows (Lines 418–421): “REDD1 can also promote senescence by regulating NF-κB-
responsive senescence genes, including Apod, Gadd45, Bcl2, and Prkcd25, independently of
miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p; this suggests that REDD1 induces vascular dysfunction via
atypical NF-κB-dependent mechanisms.”
Comment #2: REDD1 can induce cell senescence directly with mechanisms not only involving
NF-κB signaling and eNOS.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for highlighting that REDD1 may induce EC senescence
through mechanisms beyond NF-κB and eNOS/SIRT1. Although we did not directly
investigate alternative pathways in this study, several mechanisms have been proposed in
previous work.
(2) We agree that REDD1 can induce vascular dysfunction independently of NF-κB, albeit
modestly. As described in the Discussion section (Lines 358–369, 376–384), this may involve
mechanisms, such as NF-κB–independent mTOR inhibition, TXNIP-mediated oxidative stress,
VEGFR-2/3 downregulation, and mitochondrial dysfunction, which are directly regulated by
REDD1. Our data suggest that mTOR inhibition is unlikely to be involved. In contrast, TXNIP-
mediated oxidative stress, VEGFR-2/3 downregulation, and mitochondrial dysfunction may be
relevant and considered as NF-κB-independent additional mechanisms.
(3) Since NF-κB can upregulate several senescence-associated genes (Ref. 25), we have
added the following information into the Discussion section (Lines 418–421). “REDD1 can
also promote senescence by regulating NF-κB-responsive senescence genes, including Apod,
Gadd45, Bcl2, and Prkcd25, independently of miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p; this suggests that
REDD1 induces vascular dysfunction via atypical NF-κB-dependent mechanisms.”
(4) Taken together, these findings indicate that the REDD1–atypical NF-κB–eNOS/SIRT1 axis
plays a central role in endothelial senescence, while NF-κB–independent mechanisms may
also contribute under specific vascular stress conditions, albeit to a lesser extent.
Comment #3: More evidence is needed in the involvement of eNOS and SIRT1.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for emphasizing the need for additional evidence on
the involvement of eNOS and SIRT1. The eNOS–NO axis and SIRT1 are well-established
regulators of endothelial senescence and vascular homeostasis (Refs. 12, 15, 17, 24, 39–41,
55). This information has now been incorporated into the Introduction, Results, and Discussion
sections.
18
(2) In this study, REDD1 was shown to suppress the expression of eNOS and SIRT1 via NF-
κB–dependent induction of miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p. REDD1 increased SA-β-gal activity
and reduced protein expression and 3′-UTR activities of eNOS and SIRT1; these effects were
reversed by DICER knockdown or miRNA inhibition, whereas miRNA mimics reproduced the
suppressive effect (Fig. 3a–c; Supplementary Figs. 4a–g and 5). These functional experiments
further showed that REDD1-induced endothelial senescence was alleviated by an NO donor
(DETA-NO) or SIRT1 overexpression, but not by a dominant-negative SIRT1, confirming the
essential roles of eNOS and SIRT1 (Fig. 2j).
(3) Furthermore, Ad-REDD1 delivery induced vascular senescence and hypertension in WT
and iNOS–/– mice but had minimal effects in eNOS–/– mice, highlighting the critical role of eNOS
in REDD1-mediated vascular dysfunction (Fig. 4; Supplementary Fig. 8d–i).
(4) Taken together, these findings provide direct and functional evidence that REDD1
promotes endothelial senescence and vascular dysfunction through NF-κB–mediated
suppression of eNOS and SIRT1, thereby directly addressing the reviewer’s concern.
Comment #4: It remains unclear why REDD1 is activated in endothelial cells due to obesity.
It might be possible that obesity-induced inflammation activates REDD1, which then induces
endothelial senescence, instead of REDD1 inducing inflammation.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Data from this study
show that REDD1 expression is elevated in the vascular endothelium of obese mice (Fig. 1a,
b), coinciding with increased circulating metabolic and adipose tissue–derived hormonal
factors (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Exposure of ECs to these factors increased REDD1
expression, miR-155-5p/miR-214-3p levels, SA-β-gal activity, and p53/p21, all of which were
attenuated by REDD1 knockdown (Fig. 1d–h; Supplementary Figs. 1e, 7). These results
indicate that metabolic and hormonal changes, rather than inflammatory cytokines, drive
REDD1 upregulation in ECs.
(2) In contrast, obesity-associated inflammatory cytokines (TNF- and IL-6) did not increase
REDD1 expression. TNF-α induced EC senescence without affecting REDD1, and its effect
was reversed by IKKβ knockdown but not by REDD1 knockdown (Supplementary Fig. 1f).
Similarly, IL-6 did not elevate REDD1 mRNA levels (Supplementary Fig. 1g).
(3) Together, these findings suggest that REDD1 activation in obesity is primarily mediated by
circulating metabolic and hormonal factors rather than inflammatory cytokines, as summarized
in Fig. 10g.
Comment #1: Line 3: SITR1 should be SIRT1.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this typo. We have corrected “SITR1” to
‘SIRT1’ in the revised manuscript.
Comment #2: Line 111: Please also test TNF-, a direct activator of NF-ΚB signaling.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We tested TNF-, a direct activator of
NF-κB signaling, in endothelial cells. The new data have been incorporated into
Supplementary Fig. 1f, and the corresponding results have been added to the revised
manuscript (Lines 120–124); “Notably, TNF-, an obesity-induced inflammatory cytokine,
increased senescence markers without inducing REDD1 expression, and these effects were
blocked by IKKβ knockdown, but not by REDD1 knockdown (Supplementary Fig. 1f).
Similarly, IL-6 failed to induce REDD1 mRNA expression (Supplementary Fig. 1g).”
Comment #3: Line 171: There is insufficient evidence to support NF-κB involvement.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for this comment. Previous dtudies (Refs. 19, 20)
showed that REDD1 atypically activates NF-κB via IB binding (Refs. 19, 20). This study
demonstrate that REDD1 overexpression results in increased NF-κB-promoter activity,
elevated miR-155-5p/miR-214-3p expression, downregulated eNOS/SIRT1 levels, and
increased SA-β-gal activity, and all these effects were inhibited by knockdown of NF-κB p65,
but not IKKβ (Fig. 2h, i; Supplementary Figs. 3–4).
(2) In addition, we newly found that HAECs and MAECs exposed to obesity-related factors,
palmitic acid and oxLDL, increased NF-κB–responsive miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p levels,
which were effectively inhibited by NF-κB p65 knockdown and substantially reduced by
REDD1 or IKKβ silencing, although residual miRNA levels remained significant
(Supplementary Fig. 7; Lines 176–183). These results indicate that REDD1, induced by
obesity-related factors, promotes EC senescence via NF-κB–dependent biogenesis of both
miRNAs targeting eNOS and SIRT1.
(3) Although not directly examined, several additional pathways have been described in the
revised manuscript to discuss the possible involvement of REDD1 in DIO-induced endothelial
and vascular dysfunction; (i) TXNIP-mediated oxidative stress, VEGFR-2/3 downregulation,
and mitochondrial dysfunction (Lines 376–384); (ii) NF-κB-responsive expression of
senescence-associated genes, such as Apod, Gadd45, Bcl2, and Prkcd (Lines 418–421);
and
20
(iii) downregulation of quaking and its downstream signaling of TERT/TERF1–p21/p16 and
VEGFA/bFGF (Lines 427–440).
(4) Together, these results indicate that REDD1 primarily drives endothelial senescence via
atypical NF-κB signaling, while additional NF-κB–independent pathways may also contribute,
highlighting its potential multifaceted role in obesity-related vascular dysfunction.
Comment #4: Line 189: The accelerated senescence due to Ad-Redd1 delivery in eNOS KO
mice suggested that the proposed mechanism of eNOS might not be important. What is the
relationship between eNOS and SIRT1? How could REDD1 regulate both of them? Any
molecular links between eNOS and SIRT1?
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Even under control
conditions (Ad-C), eNOS–/– mice exhibited markedly accelerated vascular senescence
compared with WT mice (Supplementary Fig. 7d–i), highlighting the critical role of eNOS in
vascular homeostasis. Notably, REDD1 delivery in eNOS–/– mice reduced SIRT1 levels and
aggravated senescence, indicating that REDD1 promotes vascular senescence not only via
eNOS loss but also through suppression of SIRT1 expression.
(2) Mechanistically, REDD1 upregulates miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p, which post-
transcriptionally suppress both eNOS and SIRT1 levels (Fig. 3f–i; Supplementary Fig. 4f–k).
In the revised Discussion (Lines 401–404), we further clarify the crosstalk between eNOS and
SIRT1: they form a reciprocal regulatory loop, in which SIRT1 enhances NO production via
eNOS deacetylation (Ref. 40), and NO reciprocally sustains SIRT1 expression (Refs. 16, 24),
creating a positive feedback loop essential for vascular homeostasis. REDD1 disrupts this
SIRT1–eNOS loop, suppressing NO–cGMP signaling and thereby linking metabolic stress to
endothelial dysfunction.
Comment #1: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed
reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review
and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review
manuscripts.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your participation in the co-review process as part of the
Nature Communications initiative. We are grateful for your contribution and for supporting the
training of Early Career Researchers in peer review.
This is a comprehensive and well-executed study identifying REDD1 as a central regulator of
obesity-induced endothelial dysfunction and hypertension through an atypical NF-κB–miRNA–
eNOS/SIRT1 axis. The authors demonstrate the molecular and phenotypic consequences of
REDD1 activation using an elegant combination of in vitro endothelial models and multiple
genetically modified mouse lines (Redd1–/–, Redd1ΔEC, Redd1KKAA, and miR-214-3p–/–). The
work provides significant mechanistic insight into how metabolic stressors modulate vascular
aging and function and has clear translational relevance to obesity-related cardiovascular
disease.
Major Comments:
Comment #1: Limited Vascular Phenotyping in Resistance Arteries: While the study
thoroughly characterizes REDD1-mediated vascular changes in the aorta, this vessel is
primarily a conduit artery and does not directly regulate systemic blood pressure. Since
resistance arteries (e.g., mesenteric, renal arterioles) are key determinants of vascular tone
and blood pressure, the absence of functional and molecular assessments in these vessels
limits the physiological relevance of the findings. It would significantly strengthen the
manuscript to include data on vasomotor responses, NO bioavailability, and eNOS
expression/activity in resistance arteries from the same mouse models.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for emphasizing the role of resistance arteries. To
address this, we examined mesenteric arteries after Ad-REDD1 or Ad-REDD1KKAA
administration. Ad-REDD1 impaired ACh-mediated vasorelaxation in both thoracic aortic and
mesenteric arterial rings, whereas Ad-REDD1KKAA had no significant effect (Fig. 4g).
Consistently, REDD1-dependent impairment was observed in both vessels from DIO-WT but
not DIO-Redd1–/– mice (Fig. 6f). Experiments using an NO donor (SNP) and an NOS inhibitor
(L-NAME) confirmed preserved NO-mediated responses despite reduced eNOS–cGMP
signaling (Fig. 6g; Supplementary Fig. 9b).
(2) We further examined ACh-induced vasorelaxation in mesenteric arterial rings from DIO-
Redd1fl/fl and DIO-Redd1ΔEC-post mice (EC-specific Redd1 deletion induced after obesity) and
observed significantly improved vasorelaxation in DIO-Redd1ΔEC-post mice (Supplementary
Fig. 11h). Although mesenteric arteries could not be assessed in all experimental groups, the
available data clearly demonstrate that REDD1 also suppresses eNOS-dependent
vasorelaxation in resistance arteries. These findings extend the physiological relevance of our
study, showing that REDD1 regulates vascular tone and blood pressure in both conduit and
23
resistance arteries. Relevant statements have been incorporated into the Results sections
(Lines 197–200, 248–251, 290–293).
Comment #2: Kidney Function and Pathology Not Evaluated: Given the central role of the
renal vasculature in blood pressure regulation, the manuscript would benefit from analysis of
renal function and histopathology. Data on glomerular structure, fibrosis, proteinuria, serum
creatinine, and eNOS levels in renal tissue would offer critical insight into whether REDD1
influences hypertension through renal mechanisms in addition to vascular effects.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for highlighting the importance of assessing renal
function and histopathology in obesity-induced vascular dysfunction. To address this, we
analyzed renal structure and function in lean and DIO mice of all genotypes (WT, Redd1–/–,
Redd1ΔEC, and miR-214-3p–/–). In DIO-WT mice, we observed enlarged glomeruli, abnormal
renal architecture, increased renal fibrosis, elevated serum creatinine, and reduced renal
eNOS expression (Fig. 10a–f; Supplementary Fig. 12). These changes were substantially
ameliorated in Redd1–/–, Redd1ΔEC, and miR-214-3p–/– mice. Proteinuria was not assessed
due to limited samples.
(2) These results indicate that endothelial REDD1 activation under DIO contributes to renal
structural and functional abnormalities, likely exacerbating blood pressure elevation in addition
to its vascular effects. Statements reflecting these results have been incorporated in the
Results sections (Lines 315–323).
Comment #3: Lack of Human Validation: While the preclinical models are robust, no data
from human samples are presented to confirm the upregulation of REDD1 or its downstream
effectors (miR-155-5p, miR-214-3p, eNOS, SIRT1) in obesity-related hypertension. Inclusion
of data from human endothelial cells, vascular tissue, or patient serum (even observational)
would enhance the translational relevance of the findings.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for emphasizing the importance of validating our
findings in human samples. Although direct analysis of clinical specimens was not performed,
previous studies (Refs. 38, 43, 46, 48, 49, 57–62) report molecular changes consistent with
observations from this study. Specifically, REDD1, miR-155-5p, and miR-214-3p are elevated,
whereas eNOS and SIRT1 are reduced in serum and vascular tissues of obese, hypertensive,
or metabolically diseased individuals (Refs. 38, 48, 49, 57–62).
(2) These clinical observations support the translational relevance of the REDD1–atypical NF-
κB–miRNA axis, suggesting that the mechanisms identified in preclinical models likely
contribute to human obesity-associated vascular dysfunction. Statements reflecting this
24
discussion have been incorporated into the Discussion section (Lines 449–458).
Comment #4: Sex-Specific Differences Not Addressed: All animal experiments appear to
have been conducted exclusively in male mice, which overlooks potential sex-specific
differences in REDD1 expression, endothelial aging, and hypertensive responses. Including
female cohorts or, at a minimum, discussing this limitation is recommended to improve the
generalizability of the results.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. All experiments were
performed exclusively in male mice to minimize confounding hormonal effects and ensure
consistency of metabolic and vascular phenotypes. This has been indicated in the Abstract,
Results, and Materials and Methods sections. The Discussion (Lines 472–474) now states:
“First, all experiments were conducted in male mice, and future studies are warranted to
determine whether similar mechanisms occur in females, considering sex-related
physiological differences.” These revisions clarify the sex-specific scope of our study and
highlight the importance of investigating female models in future work.
Minor Comments:
Comment #1: DAF-FM DA as a Surrogate for NO Production: The authors use DAF-FM DA
fluorescence to quantify NO production. While this is a common and convenient method, it
measures bioavailable NO via reaction with NO-derived intermediates (e.g., N O ) and is
2 3
considered semi-quantitative. This technique does not directly assess NOS enzymatic activity,
and the fluorescence signal may be influenced by oxidative stress and NO scavenging. To
more definitively evaluate eNOS activity, the authors should consider, or at least acknowledge,
alternative approaches such as [¹⁴C]-L-arginine to [¹⁴C]-L-citrulline conversion assays or EPR
spectroscopy for detection of authentic NO.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for highlighting the limitations of using DAF-FM DA
fluorescence to assess NO production. This method provides an indirect, semi-quantitative
measure of NOS-dependent NO generation, as the fluorescence reflects NO-derived
intermediates rather than authentic NO. To confirm NOS dependency, endothelial cells and
vascular tissues were treated with the NOS inhibitor L-NAME, which reduced DAF-FM DA
fluorescence to basal levels (Figs. 2g, 3b, 5h; Supplementary Figs. 5c, g), indicating that the
observed changes primarily reflect NOS activity.
(2) We have clarified this limitation in the Discussion (Lines 475–478): “Third, eNOS activity
25
was assessed indirectly via DAF-FM DA fluorescence, highlighting the need for more direct
methods, such as L-citrulline conversion assays or other approaches for direct NO
quantification.”
Comment #2: Limitations of Tail-Cuff Blood Pressure Measurement: The authors report
systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial pressures using a non-invasive tail-cuff system. While this
method is suitable for SBP measurements, diastolic and MAP values are often unreliable due
to methodological constraints. Suggested to remove DBP and thus mean BP in all figures.
Telemetry or intra-arterial catheterisation is the gold standard for accurate, continuous blood
pressure measurement, especially in studies assessing nuanced vascular phenotypes. The
authors are encouraged to acknowledge this limitation in the discussion.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the limitations of tail-cuff blood pressure
measurement. Accordingly, DBP and MAP have been removed from all figures, and only SBP
is now reported. To acknowledge this limitation, we have added the following statement to the
Discussion (Lines 474–475): “Second, blood pressure was measured using a tail-cuff system,
which is less precise than telemetry- or catheter-based methods.” These revisions enhance
transparency regarding the methodological constraints of our study.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The revised manuscript is much improved and contains a tremendous amount of data in
support of a critical role for REDD1 in mediating endothelial senescence and vascular
dysfunction in obese mice. The studies are timely and important to the field. While most of my
prior criticisms are well addressed, some of the key claims made within the manuscript are
still not appropriately supported by experimental data. I suggest editing the manuscript to more
accurately reflect the data or performing additional assessments to provide support for them.
Comment #1: Line 365-369: Without demonstrating the absence of a change in mTORC1
signaling, the authors should not claim the changes in senescence with REDD1KKAA are
“independent of mTORC1 inhibition”. The data are unnecessarily overstated here. While no
change in REDD1-TXNIP binding in the REDD1KKAA mutant is supportive of normal protein
folding, the concern raised previously that the K219-220 sites are localized to a previously
identified “hot-spot” on REDD1 that mediates mTORC1 suppression has not been addressed
experimentally by the data.
Response: (1) We thank the reviewer for the constructive comment. To directly address the
concern regarding mTORC1 signaling, we performed additional experiments assessing S6K
and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation. Consistent with prior studies, REDD1KKAA failed to inhibit
mTORC1 activity, as evidenced by restored phosphorylation of S6K and 4E-BP1. Despite this
lack of mTORC1 inhibition, REDD1KKAA did not significantly affect miR-155-5p, eNOS, SIRT1,
senescence markers (SA-β-gal⁺ cells, p53, and p21), or SASP genes (IL1B and IL6), and this
lack of effect was unchanged by knockdown of Raptor, a key component of mTORC1, with
only weak residual senescent features remaining. These data have been incorporated in
Figure 3jm. Together, these results demonstrate that inhibition of mTORC1 is not sufficient
to drive endothelial cell senescence, confirming that REDD1-mediated EC senescence occurs
independently of mTORC1 inhibition.
(2) Accordingly, we have revised the Results section to include (Lines 174181): “In contrast,
REDD1KK219/220AA (REDD1KKAA), which cannot activate NF-κB19,20 but still binds TXNIP
(Supplementary Fig. 6a) and failed to inhibit mTORC1 activity, as indicated by restored
phosphorylation of S6K and 4E-BP1, did not significantly affect the levels of miR-155-5p,
eNOS, SIRT1, senescence markers (SA-β-gal⁺ cells, p53, and p21), or SASP genes (IL1B
and IL6) in HAECs, although some weak senescent features remained (Fig. 3j–m;
component of mTORC1, did not alter these outcomes, suggesting that REDD1-mediated
inhibition of mTORC1 is not sufficient to drive EC senescence.”

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Vascular dysfunction, including endothelial cell (EC) senescence and hypertension, is a hallmark of metabolic syndrome, yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that metabolic stress upregulates regulated in development and DNA damage response 1 (REDD1), driving vascular dysfunction. Overexpression of REDD1, but not the REDD1KK219/220AA mutant, which cannot activate atypical NF-κB, promotes EC senescence and hypertension through NSF-κB-dependent induction of miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p. These miRNAs suppress endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) and SIRT1 expression in human and mouse ECs. In obese male mice, REDD1 and miR-214-3p are upregulated, whereas eNOS and SIRT1 are downregulated, contributing to EC senescence, renal dysfunction, and hypertension. This phenotype is alleviated in mice lacking Redd1, EC-specific Redd1, or miR-214-3p, and in mice expressing Redd1KK219/220AA, but only partially by IKKβ inhibition. These findings identify a REDD1–atypical NF-κB–miRNAs–eNOS/SIRT1 axis as a critical mediator of obesity-induced vascular dysfunction and a promising therapeutic target.

---

## Introduction

Obesity, which results from significant imbalances between caloric intake and energy expenditure, directly contributes to the development of metabolic and cardiovascular risk factors, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes, chronic inflammation, and elevated adipokines. These risk factors, in turn, lead to the onset of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) and associated mortality. Obesity, particularly when accompanied by increased visceral adiposity, is a major cause of vascular dysfunction and hypertension, accounting for as much as 65–75% of the risk for primary hypertension, also known as essential or idiopathic hypertension1.

Endothelial cells (ECs), which form the inner layer (endothelium) of blood vessels, are critical for maintaining vascular homeostasis and blood pressure. They do so by modulating relaxation, angiogenesis, inflammation, and permeability through coordinated response mechanisms to multiple sensory inputs2. EC dysfunction has been identified as one of the inciting events responsible for CVDs, including hypertension and atherosclerosis1. Vascular dysfunction has been directly linked with EC senescence, which can be induced by several factors, particularly inflammation, oxidative stress, and obesity-induced metabolic changes3.

Cellular senescence is a state of irreversible cell-cycle arrest characterized by several hallmarks, including elevated levels of anti-proliferative proteins (e.g., p53, p21, and p16), accumulation of lysosomal senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal), and the induction of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP, e.g., inflammatory cytokines and chemokines)4. Various intrinsic and extrinsic factors, such as DNA damage and oxidative stress, can trigger cellular senescence3. Obesity and metabolic abnormalities have also been reported as significant risk factors for EC senescence and vascular-associated CVDs, likely by downregulating anti-senescent genes, including endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) and SIRT15,6.

Nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) is a critical factor in inflammatory responses, cellular senescence, and aging7. It is activated by factors associated with obesity and metabolic syndrome, including oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL), hyperlipidemia, and hyperglycemia8. Moreover, NF-κB stimulates the expression of various miRNAs (e.g., miR-31-5p, miR-155-5p, and miR-214-3p) that can negatively impact vascular eNOS and SIRT1 expression levels, leading to EC senescence, anti-angiogenesis, vasoconstriction, and hypertension5,9–12. Notably, the association between obesity and increased EC senescence and hypertension has been attributed to miRNA-mediated reductions in eNOS and SIRT1 levels or nitric oxide (NO) bioavailability in humans and rodents3,5,9. Therefore, inhibiting NF-κB pathways may maintain eNOS and SIRT1 expression levels, thereby preventing EC senescence and vascular dysfunction13-15. Furthermore, exogenous NO delivery and SIRT1 overexpression can mitigate EC senescence by increasing telomerase activity and preventing telomere shortening16,17. These findings suggest that obesity induces vascular dysfunction and consequent CVDs by suppressing eNOS and SIRT1 expression via the NF-κB–miRNA axis.

Regulated in development and DNA damage 1 (REDD1), also known as DNA damage-inducible transcript 4 protein (DDIT4), is an endogenous inhibitor of mechanistic target of rapamycin in complex 1 (mTORC1) and an atypical activator of NF-κB. Its genetic response is triggered by obesity, metabolic abnormalities, and factors associated with metabolic syndrome, making it a significant factor in adipogenesis, inflammation, type 2 diabetes, and EC dysfunction17. Recent studies have shown that REDD1 plays an important role in inducing metabolic inflammation in obese mice by activating the atypical NF-κB pathway by binding to and sequestering IκB without activating IKK, a key mediator in the canonical and non-canonical NF-κB pathways18–20. In addition, REDD1 expression is elevated in the brains of aged mice, senescent ECs, and doxorubicin-exposed cardiomyocytes, and its knockdown can prevent EC senescence21–23, suggesting its involvement in the pathogenesis of EC senescence. While these findings indicate that REDD1 may contribute to EC senescence associated with CVD, the mechanisms linking REDD1 with obesity-induced vascular dysfunction remain unclear.

In this study, we investigated the pathogenic role of REDD1 and the molecular mechanisms underlying its role in EC senescence and hypertension in cultured ECs and mouse models under obesity-related conditions. Our results showed that REDD1 plays a central role in the pathogenesis of obesity-induced EC senescence and hypertension by stimulating NF-κB-dependent miR-155-5p/214-3p expression, subsequently downregulating eNOS and SIRT1 expression levels.

---

## Results

Metabolic factors promote REDD1-dependent EC senescence.
As reported previously20, male mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 16 weeks to induce diet-induced obesity (DIO) exhibited increased body weight and elevated serum levels of metabolic syndrome-inducing factors (e.g., leptin, resistin, high glucose, cholesterol, oxLDL, triglycerides, and free fatty acids) compared with lean mice fed a chow diet (Supplementary Fig. 1a). REDD1 expression was markedly increased in the intact aorta of DIO mice but reduced after endothelial removal (Fig. 1a, b and Supplementary Fig. 1b), confirming endothelial-specific REDD1 expression. Immunostaining confirmed its predominant localization in aortic ECs (Fig. 1c). In cultured human aortic endothelial cells (HAECs), treatment with the metabolic risk factors, including palmitic acid, cholesterol, leptin, resistin, oxLDL, or high glucose, significantly induced REDD1 expression (Fig. 1d, e and Supplementary Fig. 1c). Treatment with palmitic acid, oxLDL, high glucose, or resistin promoted EC senescence, as evidenced by increased SA-β-gal⁺ cells and the senescence markers p53 and p21, whereas siRNA-mediated knockdown of REDD1 prevented these changes (Fig. 1f–h and Supplementary Fig. 1d, e). Given that REDD1 activates NF-B18, we investigated its role in EC senescence. IKKβ knockdown partially suppressed the increases in SA-β-gal activity induced by palmitic acid, high glucose, or resistin, with weaker inhibitory effects for high glucose or resistin than for palmitic acid; however, NF-κB p65 knockdown more effectively, though not completely, blocked SA-β-gal activity induced by these metabolic factors (Supplementary Fig. 1f).

Notably, TNF-α, an obesity-induced inflammatory cytokine, increased senescence markers without inducing REDD1 expression, and these effects were blocked by IKKβ knockdown, but not by REDD1 knockdown (Supplementary Fig. 1g). Similarly, IL-6 failed to induce REDD1 mRNA expression (Supplementary Fig. 1h). Replicative (passage-dependent) and oxidative (H₂O₂) stress also increased REDD1, p53, and p21 together with SA-β-gal activity (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). These findings suggest that REDD1 mediates EC senescence in response to metabolic, replicative, and oxidative stress, but not to classical inflammatory NF-κB activators, such as TNF-α.

REDD1 induces EC senescence via NF-κB–SIRT1/eNOS axis.
Adenoviral overexpression of REDD1 suppressed the anti-senescence protein SIRT1, increased acetylated and nuclear p53, and upregulated p21 (Fig. 2a, b), resulting in elevated SA-β-gal+ cells (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 3a). REDD1 also induced SASP gene expression, such as IL1B, IL6, IL8, and CCL2 mRNAs (Fig. 2d), as well as EC-specific SASP markers, including intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) and vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1) (Fig. 2e). Since REDD1 can atypically activate NF-κB20, which negatively regulates eNOS9,10, we examined its effects on the eNOS–NO axis and NF-κB activation. REDD1 overexpression reduced eNOS expression and NO production, which was abolished by the NOS-specific inhibitor NG-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME) (Fig. 2f, g). Notably, knockdown of NF-κB p65, but not IKKβ, inhibited REDD1-mediated NF-B promoter activity (Supplementary Fig. 3b, c) and attenuated REDD1-induced changes in eNOS, SIRT1, p53/p21, SA-β-gal activity, and IL-6 mRNA levels, although residual SA-β-gal activity and IL-6 mRNA levels remained significantly elevated (Fig. 2h, i and Supplementary Fig. 3d–f). Furthermore, REDD1-mediated EC senescence was effectively reversed by the NO donor DETA-NO and by SIRT1 overexpression, but not by its dominant-negative (DN) mutant (Fig. 2j and Supplementary Fig. 3g, h). These results suggest that REDD1 promotes EC senescence primarily via the IKKβ-independent NF-κB–SIRT1/eNOS pathway.

REDD1 downregulates eNOS and SIRT1 via NF-κB-responsive miRNAs.
Given that NF-κB-responsive miRNAs can downregulate eNOS and SIRT15,9,12, we evaluated their role in REDD1-mediated EC senescence. Knockdown of DICER, a key enzyme for miRNA biosynthesis, substantially reversed the REDD1-induced suppression of eNOS, SIRT1, and NO production, and the increase in intracellular NO was abolished by L-NAME treatment (Fig. 3a, b and Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). DICER knockdown also attenuated REDD1-mediated increases in SA-β-gal activity, miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p levels, and IL6 mRNA levels; however, SA-β-gal activity and IL6 mRNA levels remained partially but significantly elevated (Fig. 3c–e and Supplementary Fig. 4c). As both miRNAs are regulated by NF-κB activation9,11, REDD1-mediated increases in miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p levels were suppressed by knockdown of NF-κB p65, but not IKKβ (Supplementary Fig. 4d, e), suggesting that REDD1 promotes miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p biogenesis via atypical NF-κB activation. TargetScan predicted that these miRNAs target the 3′-UTRs of eNOS and SIRT1 in a species-specific manner (Supplementary Fig. 4f). We therefore assessed the effects of REDD1 on both genes in HAECs and mouse aortic endothelial cells (MAECs) using wild-type (WT) and miRNA target site-mutant 3′-UTR constructs (Supplementary Fig. 4g). Luciferase reporter assays confirmed that REDD1 inhibited NOS3 and SIRT1 3′-UTRs in a miRNA binding site-dependent and cell type-specific manner (Supplementary Fig. 4h, i). Treatment with miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p inhibitors reversed REDD1-induced eNOS/SIRT1 suppression, NO reduction, SA-β-gal activity, and IL6 mRNA upregulation, whereas their mimics reproduced the REDD1-like effects in HAECs and MAECs (Fig. 3f–i; Supplementary Figs. 4j, k, 5a–h). In contrast, REDD1KK219/220AA (REDD1KKAA), which cannot activate NF-κB19,20 but still binds TXNIP, a REDD1-interacting protein18 (Supplementary Fig. 6a) and failed to inhibit mTORC1 activity, as indicated by restored phosphorylation of S6K and 4E-BP1, did not significantly affect the levels of miR-155-5p, eNOS, SIRT1, senescence markers (SA-β-gal⁺ cells, p53, and p21), or SASP genes (IL1B and IL6) in HAECs, although some weak senescent features remained (Fig. 3j–m; Supplementary Fig. 6b, c). Notably, knockdown of RPTOR, which encodes Raptor, a key component of mTORC1, did not alter these outcomes, suggesting that REDD1-mediated inhibition mTORC1 is not sufficient to drive EC senescence. In addition, REDD1, but not REDD1KKAA, decreased the levels of phosphorylated Rb and cyclins D/E, without affecting cyclins A/B, consistent with G1-phase cell-cycle arrest associated with senescence (Supplementary Fig. 6d–g). We next examined the effects of obesity-related factors on NF-κB-responsive miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p expression. Palmitic acid and oxLDL increased these miRNAs in HAECs and MAECs, and this induction was effectively inhibited by NF-κB p65 knockdown and substantially reduced by REDD1 or IKKβ silencing, although residual miRNA levels remained significant (Supplementary Fig. 7a, b). These results suggest that REDD1, induced by obesity-related factors, promotes EC senescence through the atypical and canonical NF-κB-dependent miR-155-5p and miR-214-3p pathways, resulting in eNOS and SIRT1 downregulation.

REDD1, but not REDD1KKAA, induces vascular dysfunction in vivo.
To investigate the in vivo role of REDD1 in vascular dysfunction, male mice were intravenously injected with adenovirus encoding REDD1 (Ad-REDD1) or its mutant form (Ad-REDD1KKAA). In both groups, Redd1 mRNA levels were comparably upregulated across most tissues, showing the highest levels in the liver, markedly increased expression in the heart and aorta, and minimal expression in adipose tissue (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Serum levels of obesity-related factors, such as leptin, resistin, and triglycerides, showed no significant changes, whereas TNF-α was elevated only in Ad-REDD1-injected mice (Supplementary Fig. 8b). Unlike that of Ad-REDD1KKAA, systemic delivery of Ad-REDD1 increased SA-β-gal+ staining in the aorta, particularly in the aortic endothelium, and elevated miR-214-3p levels in mouse aortic tissues compared with Ad-Control (Fig. 4a, b). Similarly, Ad-REDD1 delivery reduced eNOS and SIRT1 expression while upregulating p53 and SASP markers, including ICAM-1 protein as well as Il1b, Il6, and Vcam1 mRNAs (Fig. 4c–e). Ad-REDD1, but not Ad-REDD1KKAA, decreased aortic NO and cGMP levels, impaired vasorelaxation of thoracic aortic and mesenteric arterial rings in response to acetylcholine (ACh), and increased systolic blood pressure (SBP), without affecting heart rate (Fig. 4f–h and Supplementary Fig. 8c). The role of eNOS in REDD1-mediated vascular senescence and hypertension was further evaluated using Nos3−/− mice. Compared with WT mice treated with Ad-control, Nos3−/− mice receiving Ad-control exhibited higher aortic SA-β-gal activity and p53 expression, without changes in SIRT1 levels. Upon Ad-REDD1 delivery in Nos3−/−mice, SIRT1 levels were reduced and p53 expression was markedly enhanced (Supplementary Fig. 8d, e). Although miR-214-3p increased after REDD1 overexpression in Nos3−/− mice, vascular NO and cGMP production remained unchanged, ACh-induced aortic vasorelaxation continued to be impaired, and SBP remained elevated (Supplementary Fig. 8f–i). In Nos2−/− mice, Ad-REDD1 delivery increased SA-β-gal activity and p53 expression, elevated vascular miR-214-3p, suppressed eNOS and SIRT1 expression, reduced vascular NO and cGMP production, impaired ACh-induced aortic vasorelaxation, and elevated SBP (Supplementary Fig. 8j–p). These results suggest that REDD1 overexpression induces vascular senescence and hypertension in vivo, accompanied by increased miR-214-3p levels and decreased eNOS and SIRT1 expression.

Redd1 loss attenuates DIO-induced vascular senescence and hypertension.
Given the critical role of REDD1 in metabolic disorders, including obesity and type 2 diabetes18,20, we assessed its contribution to vascular senescence and blood pressure in obese male mice. Compared with their lean counterparts, DIO-WT mice showed increased SA-β-gal+ staining in the aortas, especially in the endothelium, and this increase was reduced in DIO-Redd1−/− mice (Fig. 5a). Consistent with these findings, DIO elevated miR-214-3p expression in the aortas and serum of WT mice compared with that in lean controls, which was lower in DIO-Redd1−/− mice (Fig. 5b). Confocal imaging and biochemical analysis showed that DIO increased REDD1 levels and decreased eNOS and SIRT1 expression in the aortic endothelium of WT mice, accompanied by elevated total and acetylated p53, senescence markers (p53, p21, and p16), and SASP mRNAs (Il1b, Il6, and Vcam1) (Fig. 5c–g). These changes were attenuated in DIO- Redd1−/− mice, indicating that REDD1 plays a key role in DIO-induced vascular senescence. Moreover, DIO-WT mice demonstrated reduced aortic NO and cGMP production compared with their lean controls, and these levels were partially restored in DIO-Redd1−/− mice, with the recovery abolished by L-NAME (Fig. 5h). Consistently, ACh-mediated aortic vasorelaxation responses were impaired in DIO-WT aortas but improved in DIO-Redd1−/− mice (Fig. 5i). Likewise, SBP was higher in DIO-WT mice than in lean controls, and this effect was partially, but significantly, reduced in DIO-Redd1−/− mice (Fig. 5j). Notably, lean WT and Redd1−/− mice showed no significant differences, whereas DIO-Redd1−/− mice exhibited significantly impaired vascular function compared with lean Redd1−/− mice (Fig. 5b, e–j). These results indicate that REDD1 deficiency is associated with reduced obesity-induced EC senescence and hypertension, with partial reduction of miR-214-3p levels and partial restoration of eNOS, and SIRT1 expression, suggesting that REDD1 contributes to, but does not solely drive, these phenotypes.

More vascular protection by Redd1 deletion than IKK inhibition.
Given the established role of canonical NF-κB signaling in obesity-induced CVDs8, we compared the relative contributions of REDD1-mediated atypical NF-κB activation and IKK-dependent canonical NF-κB signaling in DIO-associated vascular dysfunction. Treatment with the IKK inhibitor Bay 11-7082 reduced vascular senescence and molecular alterations in both DIO-WT and DIO-Redd1−/− mice, as reflected by reduced SA-β-gal+ staining, suppression of miR-214 upregulation, partial restoration of eNOS and SIRT1, attenuation of p53 protein and Il6 and Vcam1 mRNA levels, and improved NO-cGMP signaling (Fig. 6a–e and Supplementary Fig. 9a). Bay 11-7082 also partially restored ACh-induced vasorelaxation in thoracic aortic and mesenteric arterial rings in both groups, an effect abolished by L-NAME, whereas the NO donor sodium nitroprusside induced comparable maximal relaxation across groups (Fig. 6f, g and Supplementary Fig. 9b). Moreover, Bay 11-7082 attenuated the DIO-induced elevation in SBP in both genotypes (Fig. 6h). Notably, the protective effects of Bay 11-7082 in DIO-WT mice were less pronounced than those observed in untreated DIO-Redd1−/− mice (Fig. 6a–f, h and Supplementary Fig. 9a, b), suggesting that the REDD1-mediated atypical NF-κB activation may play a more important role than the canonical NF-κB pathway in mediating obesity-induced vascular senescence and hypertension.

Redd1KKAA mice are protected from DIO-induced vascular dysfunction.
To delineate the role of atypical NF-κB activation by REDD1, we analyzed Redd1KKAA mice. Consistent with previous findings20, DIO increased circulating levels of leptin, resistin, glucose, cholesterol, triglycerides, free fatty acids, and TNF-α in WT mice, but these elevations were attenuated in Redd1KKAA mice, with no significant differences observed between genotypes under lean conditions (Supplementary Fig. 10a). Under DIO conditions, Redd1KKAA mice showed reduced SA-β-gal+ staining in the aortic endothelium (Fig. 7a) and were protected from the DIO-induced miR-214-3p upregulation in both aortic and serum measurements (Fig. 7b). Redd1KKAA mice maintained eNOS and SIRT1 expression and showed reduced senescence and SASP markers (p53, p21, p16, Il1a, Il1b, Il6, and Vcam1) under DIO conditions (Fig. 7c–e), leading to improved NO and cGMP production, enhanced ACh-induced aortic vasorelaxation, and attenuated SBP elevation (Fig. 7f–h). In contrast, lean mice showed no such changes (Fig. 7a–h). These results suggest that REDD1 promotes obesity-induced EC senescence and hypertension primarily through the atypical NF-κB–miR-214-3p–eNOS/SIRT1 axis, while also modulating systemic metabolic parameters as reported previously20.

Redd1ΔEC mice are protected from DIO-induced vascular dysfunction.
To define the role of endothelial REDD1, we examined Redd1ΔEC mice. DIO increased the serum levels of obesity-associated and inflammatory factors similarly in WT and Redd1ΔEC mice, with no statistically significant differences between genotypes (Supplementary Fig. 10b). Nonetheless, DIO-induced SA-β-gal+ staining in the aortic endothelium was attenuated in Redd1ΔEC mice (Fig. 8a). Endothelial deletion of REDD1 also mitigated aortic miR-214-3p induction, although the corresponding serum effect was less pronounced (Fig. 8b). Consequently, eNOS and SIRT1 expression, which were reduced in DIO-Redd1fl/fl mice, were partially preserved in DIO-Redd1ΔEC mice (Fig. 8c). Similarly, senescence-associated markers (p53, acetylated p53, p21, and p16) and SASPs (Il1a, Il1b, Il6, and Vcam1) were also attenuated in DIO-Redd1ΔEC mice (Fig. 8c–e). Consistent with these findings, Redd1ΔEC mice exhibited improved vascular NO and cGMP production, ACh-induced aortic vasorelaxation, and SBP under DIO conditions (Fig. 8f–h). These protective effects were not observed in lean controls (Fig. 8a–h). To assess the therapeutic relevance of endothelial Redd1 deletion, post-obesity EC-specific (DIO-Redd1ΔEC-post) mice were generated after confirming obesity by serum leptin and triglyceride measurements following 14 weeks of HFD feeding (Supplementary Fig. 11a, b). Two weeks later, assessment revealed significant improvements in vascular senescence, ACh-induced mesenteric arterial vasorelaxation, blood pressure, and related molecular markers compared with DIO-Redd1fl/fl controls (Supplementary Fig. 11c–i), closely resembling the protective effects observed in DIO-Redd1ΔEC mice. These results suggest that endothelial REDD1 is an important mediator of DIO-induced vascular senescence and hypertension, independent of systemic metabolic alterations.

miR-214-3p deficiency alleviates DIO-induced vascular dysfunction.
To determine the role of miR-214-3p in vascular dysfunction, we used miR-214-3p−/− mice. HFD feeding similarly increased obesity-associated serum factors in WT and miR-214-3p−/− mice, with no significant differences between genotypes (Supplementary Fig. 10c). However, SA-β-gal+ staining in the aortic endothelium was markedly attenuated in DIO-miR-214-3p−/− mice compared with that in DIO-WT mice, whereas no significant differences were observed under lean conditions (Fig. 9a). MiR-214-3p was upregulated in the aorta and serum of DIO-WT mice, but remained undetectable in miR-214-3p−/− mice (Fig. 9b). Under DIO conditions, REDD1 expression increased similarly in the aortas of both genotypes; however, reductions of eNOS and SIRT1 and elevations of p53, p21, and p16 were observed only in DIO-WT mice (Fig. 9c). Thus, DIO-induced elevations in Il1a, Il1b, Il6, and Vcam1 were attenuated in miR-214-3p−/− mice (Fig. 9d, e). Furthermore, miR-214-3p deletion partially restored DIO-mediated reductions in vascular NO−cGMP signaling and ACh-induced aortic vasorelaxation of thoracic aortic rings (Fig. 9f, g), thereby ameliorating SBP elevation (Fig. 9h). These results suggest that miR-214-3p contributes to obesity-induced vascular dysfunction in DIO mice, including EC senescence and hypertension, at least in part through modulation of eNOS and SIRT1 expression.

Redd1 and miR-214-3p deletion mitigates DIO-induced renal dysfunction.
Given the crucial role of the renal vasculature in blood pressure regulation, we assessed whether the REDD1-miR-214 axis contributes to renal dysfunction under DIO conditions. In WT, DIO caused glomerulomegaly, renal fibrosis, and elevated serum creatinine, whereas these pathological changes were effectively attenuated in Redd1−/−, Redd1ΔEC, and miR-214-3p−/− mice (Fig. 10a–e and Supplementary Fig. 12). These mice also exhibited partial preservation of eNOS expression under DIO conditions (Fig. 10f). Collectively, these findings suggest that REDD1 contributes to DIO-induced renal dysfunction, a potential contributor to hypertension, via NF-κB-responsive miR-214-3p-mediated modulation of eNOS.

## Methods

Cell culture and treatment
HAECs (#6100) and human aortic smooth muscle cells (HASMCs, #6110) were obtained from ScienCell Research Labs (San Diego, CA, USA). MAECs were obtained from iXcells Biotechnologies (#10MU-002, San Diego, CA, USA). ECs were cultured in EGM-2 medium (#CC-3156; Walkersville, MA, USA) supplemented with growth factors (#CC-4176; Lonza Bioscience) or EC growth medium (#MD-0010, iXcells Biotechnologies), whereas HASMCs were cultured in smooth muscle cell medium (#1101, ScienCell Research Labs). For studies involving replicative senescence, HAECs (1.5 × 104 cells/cm2) were cultured in M199 media (#11043023; Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA)10, and serially passaged using trypsinization with trypsin‐EDTA (#25200072, Gibco, Grand Island, NY, USA) when the cells reached approximately 80–90% confluence13. To determine premature senescence, ECs between passages 4 and 5 were transfected with siRNAs (80 nM, control siRNA, #sc-37007; human REDD1, #sc-45806; mouse Redd1, #sc-45807; human IKKβ, #sc-35644; human NF-κB p65, #sc-29410; mouse NF-κB p65, #sc-29411; human Raptor, #44069; human DICER, #sc40489; San Cruz Biotechnology), miRNA mimics or inhibitors (80 nM, Supplementary Table 1), pFLAG-REDD1 (1 µg DNA/ml)19, or plasmid DNAs (1 µg/ml; human WT or DN mutant H363Y SIRT1; Plasmid #1791, Addgene, Watertown, MA, USA) using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX or Lipofectamine 3 000 (Invitrogen). Cells were then treated with or without oxLDL (50 µg/ml), prepared by incubating native LDL (1.019 mg protein) with 10 µM CuSO4 for 4 h64, cholesterol (100 µM, #C8667; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), glucose (25 mM, 25 mM L-glucose used for osmotic control), recombinant human resistin (100 ng/ml, #1359-RN; R&D systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA), recombinant human leptin (10 µg/ml, #398-LP; R&D Systems), recombinant human TNF-α (10 ng/ml, #10291-TA; R&D Systems), recombinant human IL-6 (40 ng/ml, #206-IL; R&D Systems), palmitate-BSA (300 µM), or H2O2 (50−150 µM) for 48 h. Palmitic acid-BSA solution (5 mM) was prepared by mixing 10 µL of palmitate solution (500 mM in ethanol, #P9767; Sigma-Aldrich) with 1 mL of BSA solution (10%, w/v in serum-free M199, #A8806; Sigma-Aldrich). Subsequently, the solution was filtered through a 0.22 µm pore size membrane filter (Millipore, Billerica, MA) and stored at −80°C until use. For some experiments, ECs were infected with control adenovirus (Ad-Ctrl) or adenoviral REDD1 (Ad-REDD1, 50−150 MOI).

Animal study
C57BL/6J (#000664: B6/J), Nos3−/− (#002684; B6.129P2-Nos3/J), and Nos2−/− (#002609; B6.129P2-Nos2tm1Lau/J) mice were obtained from The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME). VE-cadherin-CreERT2 (#13073; C57BL/6-Tg(Cdh5-cre/ERT2)1Rha) mice were purchased from Taconic Biosciences (Rensselaer, NY, USA). Redd1−/−, Redd1KKAA, Redd1flox/flox (Redd1fl/fl), and miR-214-3p−/− mice were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 on a C57BL/6J genetic background20. Mice were housed in a pathogen-free animal facility (temperature, 18–24°C; humidity, 30–50%) with a 12:12 h light/dark cycle. Endothelial-specific Redd1-deficient (Redd1ΔEC) mice were generated by crossing Redd1fl/fl with VE-cadherin-CreERT2 mice and intraperitoneally administering 100 µL of tamoxifen solution (20 mg/ml stock solution in corn oil) once every 24 h for 5 consecutive days. Six- to eight-week-old male mice were randomized into two groups and fed either a chow diet (10 kcal% fat, #D12450B, Research diets/Joongah Bio, Suwon, Republic of Korea; lean mouse) or an HFD (60 kcal% fat, #D12492, Research diets/Joongah Bio; DIO mouse) for 16 weeks. To establish post-obesity EC-specific (DIO-Redd1ΔEC-post) mice, VE-cadherin-CreERT2:Redd1fl/fl mice were intraperitoneally injected with tamoxifen following 14 weeks of an HFD-induced DIO. To study the role of canonical NF-κB, DIO-WT and DIO- Redd1−/− mice were administered intraperitoneal injections of Bay 11-7082 (5 mg/kg, dissolved in 1% DMSO) or vehicle every other day for the last two weeks. In addition, 14-week-old male WT, Nos3−/−, and Nos2−/− mice were intravenously injected with Ad-C or Ad-REDD1 (1 × 109 plaque-forming units in a total volume of 10 µl/mice) and maintained for 12 days. Following anesthesia with an intraperitoneal injection of Avertin (200 mg/kg), blood samples were collected from the abdominal aorta, centrifuged at 3,000 × g for 10 min at 4°C, and immediately stored at −80°C. The aortas and mesenteric arteries were rapidly and carefully isolated to evaluate vascular senescence, vascular relaxation response, the eNOS/NO pathway, and the expression levels of various genes. All experiments were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Kangwon National University (approval numbers: KW-210630-1 and KW-210707-6) and were carried out in accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (8th edition, NIH, USA).

SA-β-gal staining and immunohistochemistry
EC and aortic vessel senescence were assessed using the Senescence β-Galactosidase Staining Kit (#9860, Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Images of the stained ECs were captured using an Olympus IX71P phase-contrast inverted microscope, and the percentage of SA-β-gal+ senescent cells was quantified in three separate fields using ImageJ software (v1.53c, NIH). Mouse aortas were fixed, washed with ice-cold phosphate buffered saline (PBS), and incubated with β-gal staining solution. Images of the stained aortic vessels were captured using a digital camera. Aortic vessels were embedded in optimum cutting temperature (OCT) compound and sectioned every 8 µm from the middle portion of the descending thoracic aorta to the diaphragm using a cryostat microtome (HM525NX, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Images of SA-β-gal-stained aortic sections were acquired using the Digital Slide Scanner (Ocus®40, Grundium Ltd., Finland). For immunohistochemistry, fresh aortic vessels embedded in OCT compound were sectioned at a thickness of 10 µm using a cryostat microtome. These sections were stained with an anti-CD31 antibody (1:100, #AF3628, RRID: AB_2161028; R&D Systems) and a donkey anti-goat IgG (H+L)-Alexa Fluor™ 647 (1:100, #ab150131, RRID: AB_2732857; Abcam, Boston, MA, USA) for EC analysis; an anti-α-SMA antibody (1:100, #A5228, RRID: AB_262054; Sigma-Aldrich) and a goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L)-Alexa Fluor™ 405 (1:100, #A-31553, RRID: AB_221604; Invitrogen) for vascular smooth muscle cell analysis; an anti-REDD1 antibody (1:100, #10638-1-AP, RRID: AB_2245711; Proteintech, Rosemont, IL, USA) and a goat anti-rabbit IgG (H+L)-Alexa Fluor™ 488 (1:100, #A-11006, RRID: AB_2576217; Invitrogen) for REDD1 expression analysis; and an anti-eNOS antibody (1:100, #PA1-037, RRID: AB_325774; Invitrogen) and goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L)-Alexa Fluor™ 405 (1:100, #A-31553, RRID: AB_221604; Invitrogen) for eNOS analysis. Fluorescence images of the slides were captured using a confocal laser scanning microscope (LSM-880, Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany).

Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Masson’s Trichrome staining
Kidney tissues were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at a thickness of 5 µm using a microtome (Microm HM 340E, Thermo Scientific, Walldorf, Germany). Sections were then deparaffinized, rehydrated, and stained with H&E or a Trichrome stain kit (#ab150686, Abcam) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Images were acquired using a digital slide scanner (Ocus®40, Grundium Ltd. Tampere, Finland), and glomerular size and fibrotic area were quantified in four randomly selected fields per section using the ImageJ software (NIH).

Measurement of glucose, cytokines, adipokines, and lipids
Blood glucose levels were measured using the Accu-Chek active blood glucose meter (Roche Diagnostics, Seoul, Republic of Korea). Plasma levels of leptin (#MOB00, R&D Systems), resistin (#MRSN00, R&D Systems), cholesterol (#BM-CDL-100, Biomax, Guri-si, Republic of Korea), triglyceride (#BM-TGR-100, Biomax), free fatty acid (BM-FFA-100, Biomax), and oxLDL (#MBS2512757, MyBiosource, San Diego, CA, USA) were analyzed using ELISA kits according to the manufacturers’ protocol.

Co-immunoprecipitation and Western blotting
Cells were suspended in RIPA buffer (ELPIS-Biotech Inc., Daejeon, Republic of Korea) and incubated on ice for 30 min for complete cell lysis19. Using a BioMasher-II homogenizer (Optima, Tokyo, Japan), aortic vessel tissues were homogenized in ice-cold protein extraction buffer containing 100 mM HEPES (pH 7.9), 10% glycerol, 5% Triton X-100, 250 mM NaF, 5 mM Na3VO4, and Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (100×, Thermo Fisher Scientific)11. Lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 10 min at 4°C, and the supernatants were collected for analysis. Total protein extracts (1 mg) were precleared with protein G plus/protein A-agarose (#IP10; Millipore) for 1 h at 4°C and then subject to co-immunoprecipitation with a FLAG M2 antibody (#F1804, RRID: AB_262044; Sigma-Aldrich). The resulting immunoprecipitates and cell lysates (30−40 µg protein) were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride membranes (#GE10600023; Cytiva, Marlborough, MA, USA). The membranes were blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA, #BSAS0.1; Bovogen Biologicals Pty Ltd., Australia) in Tris-buffered saline (50 mM Tris-Cl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl) containing 0.05% Tween-20 and analyzed using immunoblotting with the respective primary antibodies: ant-eNOS (1:1000, #PA1-037, RRID: AB_325774; Invitrogen), anti-DICER (1:1000, #5362, RRID: AB_2093073; Cell Signaling Technology), anti-IKKβ (1:1000, #2684, RRID: AB_2122298; Cell Signaling Technology), anti-REDD1 (1:1000, #10638-1-AP, RRID: AB_2245711; Proteintech), anti-p65 (1:1000, #8242T, RRID: AB_10859369; Cell Signaling Technology), anti-p53 (1:1000, #2524, RRID: AB_331743; Cell Signaling Technology), anti-acetyl-p53 (1:1000, #2570, RRID: AB_823591; Cell Signaling Technology), anti-p21 (1:1000, #SC-6246, RRID: AB_823591; Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, CA, USA), anti-p16 (1:1000, #SC-1661, RRID: AB_628067; Santa Cruz), anti-SIRT1 (1:1000, #8469S, RRID: AB_10999470; Cell Signaling Technology), anti-ICAM-1 (1:1000, #MA5407, RRID: AB_223596; Invitrogen), anti-VCAM-1 (1:1000, #MA5-31965, RRID: AB_2809259; Invitrogen), anti-Raptor (1:1000, #2280, RRID: AB_561245; Cell Signaling Technology), anti-phospho-S6K (Thr389, 1:1000, #9234, RRID: AB_2269803; Cell Signaling Technology), anti-S6K (1:1000, #34475, RRID: AB_2943679; Cell Signaling Technology), anti-phospho-4E-BP1 (Thr37/46, 1:1000, #9459, RRID: AB_330985; Cell Signaling Technology), anti-4E-BP1 (1:1000, #9452, RRID: AB_331692; Cell Signaling Technology), anti--actin (1:5000, #A5441, RRID: AB_476744; Sigma-Aldrich), anti-TXNIP (1:1000, #14715, RRID: AB_2714178, Cell Signaling Technology), or anti--tubulin (1:10000, #2144S, RRID: AB_2210548; Sigma-Aldrich). The membranes were incubated with a HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse (1:4000, #31430, RRID: APB_228307; Thermo-Fisher Scientific) or HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG antibody (1:4000, #31460, RRID: AB_228341; Thermo-Fisher Scientific). The blots were visualized using an X-ray film and an enhanced chemiluminescence kit (#34580; Thermo Scientific), and protein band intensities were quantified using the ImageJ software (NIH).

FACS analysis
HAECs were infected with 150 MOI of Ad-Control, Ad-REDD1, and Ad-REDD1KKAA for 48 h. Cells were harvested using 1 ml of 0.25% trypsin-EDTA solution, quenched with culture medium containing 5% FBS, and centrifuged at 300  g for 5 min at room temperature. The cell pellet was washed, resuspended in PBS, and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min, followed by centrifugation at 1000  g for 5 min and resuspension at 4−6  106 cells/ml in cold PBS. Cells (500 µL) were fixed by gently vortexing with the dropwise addition of 5 ml of cold 70% ethanol and stored for at least 2 h at 4°C. Fixed cells were collected, resuspended in 500 µL of permeabilization solution [100 µl of permeabilization buffer (10, #00-8333-56, Invitrogen), 50 µl of propidium iodide (#P4864, Sigma-Aldrich), and 2.5 µl of RNase A solution (#70856, 1 ml, Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) in a total volume of 1 ml PBS], and incubated in the dark for 15 min. Flow cytometry data of the stained cells (10,000 cells/sample) were acquired using the BD FACSVerse Flow Cytometer (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) and analyzed using the FlowJo software, version 10.2 (BD Biosciences). The gating strategy for cell-cycle analysis is shown in Supplementary Fig. 14.

Reporter gene assay
To evaluate eNOS promoter activity, ECs were transfected with 1 µg/ml of pGL3-human eNOS promoter (1.6 kb)-firefly luciferase construct and 500 ng/ml of Renilla luciferase pGL4.74 vector using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen)10. To analyze target gene 3-UTR-reporter activity, cells were transfected with 2 µg/ml of the psiCHECK-2 vector containing either the WT or mutant 3-UTR of eNOS (human, 430 bp; mouse, 470 bp) or SIRT1 (human, 680 bp; mouse 720 bp) using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen). Following transfection for 4 h, the cells were recovered in fresh medium for 24 h, and reporter gene activity was assessed using the Dual-Luciferase Assay Kit (#E1960, Promega, Madison, WI, USA). Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase activity.

eNOS–NO–cGMP pathway analysis
In situ aortic NO production was determined in vessel segments using a fluorescence image-based method11. Vessels were cut longitudinally, pinned to the bottom of a Sylgard-coated chamber (with the endothelial layer on top), and incubated with 5 µM 4-amino-5-methylamino-2´,7´-difluorofluorescein diacetate (DAF-FM DA, #CAS 254109-22-3, Calbiochem) in HEPES buffer for 30 min at 37C in minimal light. The chamber allowed for static bath conditions during fluorescence measurements. After washing to remove excess DAF-FM DA, fluorescence images were acquired at every 30 s for 5 min using an Olympus BX51 epifluorescence microscope with optimized excitation and emission wavelength (470/525 nm), an intensified camera (658M-TL, Luca, Los Angeles, CA, USA), and the cellSens imaging software, ver.4.1 (Olympus, Hamburg, Germany). The average fluorescence intensity was calculated from five frames (2 × 2 binning) of the entire field of view using the Metamorph software (Olympus). Slope changes in fluorescence over time were determined by linear regression using the data analysis software Origin (version 7.5, OriginLab Corp, Northampton, MA, USA), wherein one arbitrary unit of NO production was defined as a 0.1 increase of DAF fluorescence intensity/s. Furthermore, intracellular NO levels were measured in ECs treated with the NO fluorescence probe DAF-FM DA using a confocal laser scanning microscope (LSM-880, Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany)65. To evaluate cGMP production, ECs (1 × 105 cells) were transfected with 80 nM of control or miRNA inhibitors using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen) and infected with 150 MOI of Ad-C or Ad-REDD1, followed by co-culturing with HASMCs (1 × 105 cells) for 24 h48. The co-cultured media and lysates of aortic tissues isolated from mice were collected to measure cGMP levels using an ELISA kit (#KGE003; R&D Systems). The protein concentration in total lysates obtained from cells and aortic tissues was determined using a BCA method.

Measurement of blood pressure and vascular relaxation
Blood pressure was measured using the non-invasive CODA-HT4 tail-cuff system (CODA, Kent Scientific, Torrington, CT, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, each mouse was acclimated for at least 10 practice sessions for a minimum of 15 min, and blood pressure parameters were subsequently recorded. In each recording session, one set of five acclimation cycles followed by three sets of 10 acquisition cycles were performed. The average of the last 20 successful recordings was used for calculating the systolic and diastolic blood pressures and heart rates. The tail temperature was monitored before and during the measurement, and mice with a core temperature of 33–35°C were used. The vasorelaxation responses of isolated carotid and mesenteric arterial rings to acetylcholine (ACh) were assayed using a multiwire myography system (DMT-620M, Aarhus, Denmark)11. Arterial rings (≈ 2 mm in length) were mounted on tungsten wires in a myograph chamber filled with physiological salt solution maintained at 37°C and aerated with 95% O₂ and 5% CO₂. After equilibration and normalization to optimal resting tension, vessels were precontracted with phenylephrine (1 µM) to achieve approximately 70–80% of maximal contraction, followed by cumulative addition of ACh to generate concentration-response curves. Vasorelaxation was expressed as the percentage of relaxation relative to the precontracted tone.

Reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR)
Total miRNAs were isolated from cells, tissues, and serum using the miRNeasy Mini kit (#217004; Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) or the miRNeasy serum/plasma kit (#217184; Qiagen). cDNA for miRNA quantification was synthesized from 1 µg of miRNA using the miScript II RT kit (#218161; Qiagen). MiRNA levels were then quantified via qPCR using target-specific primers (Supplementary Table 1)9. MiRNA levels were normalized to the housekeeping gene SNORD95. For mRNA quantification, total RNA was extracted from cultured cells and mouse tissues using the TRIzol reagent (#15596018, Invitrogen). First-strand cDNA was synthesized using M-MLV Reverse Transcriptase (#M1705; Promega), followed by qPCR for the quantification of target gene mRNA levels using target-specific primers (Supplementary Table 2). Expression levels of target gene mRNAs were normalized to the expression of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase.

Statistics and reproducibility
Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism (version 9.0; GraphPad Software Inc.). No statistical methods were used to predetermine the sample size. The experiments were randomized, and investigators were blinded to group allocation during experiments and outcome analysis. No samples or animals were excluded from the analysis. For cell-based experiments, n represents the number of independent biological replicates, whereas for animal studies, n represents the number of mice per group, as indicated in the figure legends. All representative images were obtained from at least three independent experiments with similar results. Western blotting, SA-β-gal staining, intracellular NO measurements, and renal histological analyses were quantified using all independent replicates, with data shown in the main or Supplementary Figures. Non-quantified representative vascular images were obtained from at least three animals per group, and the corresponding numbers of biological replicates are specified in the figure legends. All values are presented as means ± standard error of the mean (s.e.m). Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05 and was determined using two-sided unpaired t-tests or two-sided multiple t-tests for comparisons between two groups or one-way or two-way ANOVA followed by the Holm–Sidak’s multiple comparisons test. Exact P values are provided in the figures wherever applicable.

Data availability
All data supporting the findings of this study are provided in the article, the Supplementary Information, and the Source Data file, including uncropped blots and the source data for all graphs in the main and supplementary figures. Additional raw data are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request.
